name: Pearl extract

lead: Pearl extract and pearl powder are made from ground pearls or nacre and used in traditional Chinese medicine and in cosmetics sold for brightening and anti-aging. People use them for a more radiant, even-looking complexion. Pearl medicine in China has a history of more than 2,000 years, and it is described as used to calm the mind, clear the eyes and soothe skin.

Laboratory and animal studies have looked at antioxidant effects, fibroblast migration, UV-exposed skin cells and photoaging in mice, and a few reports address skin lightening and melasma. Controlled human trials for appearance are limited.

paras: It is used topically in creams, masks and powders, and in traditional medicine it is also taken by mouth. Results are generally described as gradual brightening with regular use.

Sources describe it as widely used topically. Wikipedia notes oral doses in traditional medicine and that excessive amounts may cause calcium toxicity. Little safety data from controlled skin trials was found.

angle.text: Pearl extract and powder are used in traditional Chinese medicine and in cosmetics for a brighter, more radiant and even complexion. The proposed route is antioxidant and skin-cell activity; most research is in laboratory and animal studies, with few human skin trials.

lead: Pearl extract and pearl powder are preparations made from pearls or nacre, used in traditional Chinese medicine and in cosmetics marketed for brightening and anti-aging.[1][2] Pearl medicine in China has a history of more than 2,000 years, and it is described as used to calm the mind, clear the eyes and soothe skin.[3]

Published research on pearl extract in skin applications consists largely of laboratory and animal studies, such as work on fibroblast migration, UV-exposed skin cells and photoaging in mice, along with a small number of reports on skin lightening and melasma.[4][5][6][7][8] Evidence from controlled human trials for appearance outcomes is limited.

People use pearl extract in two main ways. Topically, it appears in brightening creams and masks sold as a way to even tone and add glow; orally, pearl powder is taken in traditional medicine for complexion and general wellbeing. Researchers have proposed that pearl matrix proteins may interact with pigment-forming pathways: one laboratory study reported that hydrolysed conchiolin protein from pearls antagonised both endothelin-1 and alpha-MSH, two signals involved in melanin production.[9]
infobox: Ground freshwater or low-grade saltwater pearls, or nacre[1]
Calcium carbonate (aragonite) bound by conchiolin protein, trace minerals, amino acids[10]
Powder, cream ingredient, hydrolysed protein extracts
Chinese medicine, Ayurveda, European skin whitener[1]

paras: Pearl powder is made by sterilising freshwater or low-grade saltwater pearls and milling them finely; it is sold as a powder or mixed into creams.[1] It is described as containing amino acids, trace minerals and a high concentration of calcium.[1] Pearl powder is distinguished from nacre powder, which comes from the inner layer of the shell.[3] Reviews describe extraction of matrix proteins from both as a route to cosmetic and medical ingredients.[3]

Pearls are mostly calcium carbonate, usually aragonite or an aragonite-calcite mix, laid down in concentric layers bound by conchiolin, an organic horn-like protein; aragonite plus conchiolin is called nacre, the same material as mother-of-pearl.[10] Freshwater pearls form in mussels of the family Unionidae, while saltwater pearls come from marine oysters of the family Pteriidae.[10] China is the largest freshwater pearl producer, which is why much pearl powder is freshwater-derived.[10]

Cultured-pearl farming was developed in the early twentieth century: Tokichi Nishikawa received a Japanese patent in 1916, and freshwater cultivation began in 1914 with mussels from Lake Biwa.[10] The conchiolin matrix is the part scientists extract as hydrolysed protein for cosmetic work.[3][9] Pearls have been crushed for cosmetics, medicines and paints, and Ayurvedic texts describe pearl powder as a digestive stimulant and mental tonic.[10]

Use in China is documented from at least 320 AD, and the Ming-era Bencao Gangmu is said to credit pearl powder with stimulating skin growth and reducing sun damage; Empress Wu Zetian reportedly used it.[1] It was also used in Ayurveda, and in medieval and early modern Europe for several conditions; in the 19th century it was used as a skin whitener, though one period source condemned it as harmful.[1]

Pearl extract is marketed for brightening and as an anti-aging ingredient, and is a common component of Asian skin-care products.[1] Proponents cite its traditional reputation and ingredient content; researchers describe antioxidant, anti-aging and tonic activities in laboratory settings.[2]

A paper titled "Soluble Pearl Extract provides effective skin lightening by antagonizing endothelin" reports on a proposed mechanism for lightening,[5] and a 2025 paper reports that pearl extract alleviates melasma by targeting CREB1.[7] A 2022 study examined a pearl extract from Pinctada fucata martensii in UV-induced photoaging in mice.[6]

Wikipedia describes pearl powder as made from freshwater pearls or saltwater pearls below jewellery grade: the pearls are sterilised in boiling water and milled to powder with stainless steel discs or porcelain balls in moist conditions, and the powder is sold as such or mixed into creams.[1] It is described as containing amino acids, more than 30 trace minerals and a high concentration of calcium.[1] A 2021 review of pearl powder as a biomedical material covers applications in wound healing, bone repair and skin conditions.[11] Scientists also study extracted matrix proteins from pearl and nacre as cosmetic and medical ingredients.[3]

Chinese use is said to date back at least to 320 AD, and Empress Wu Zetian (625 to 705) is reported to have used it internally and on her skin.[1] In India, the Kashmiri physician Narahari (c. 1240) described it as an antidote and a treatment for eye conditions, and a 1903 Indian pharmacological work listed it as a tonic; in Europe, Francis Bacon recommended it for prolonging life and nineteenth-century women used it as a skin whitener, though an 1838 work described it as a source of a pale, sickly hue.[1] A Philippines tradition, which Wikipedia marks as needing a citation, describes youths secluded from the sun and coated with crushed pearl powder to keep skin fair.[1]

Pearl extract enhanced migration of fibroblasts in a wound-healing model, and a pearl extract gel showed anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic effects in UVB-irradiated keratinocytes.[2][4] In mice, a pearl extract from Pinctada fucata martensii protected against UV-induced photoaging.[6] A randomised placebo-controlled trial of protein-rich pearl powder examined antioxidant status in people and lifespan in worm models.[12] A case report described a 94-year-old woman whose stage 2 pressure injury was treated with metronidazole and nano pearl powder mixed together.[13] A pilot randomised study of shell-derived calcium in postmenopausal women with low bone density studied a calcium supplement rather than skin outcomes.[14]

In skin care the ingredient appears in two broad ways: as a fine powder or extract in creams, masks and serums marketed for even tone and radiance, and as a hydrolysed protein ingredient. The appearance chain proponents describe is topical brightening: a mild antioxidant and tone-evening ingredient in routines alongside sunscreen and other actives. Laboratory papers report protection of skin cells and mouse skin against UV damage and, in a few reports, effects on melanin-related signalling, which is the mechanism cited for lightening.[4][5][6][9]

The 2023 paper on hydrolysed conchiolin protein describes antagonism of endothelin-1 and alpha-MSH, two signals that drive pigment production, and the 2025 melasma paper reports an effect through the transcription factor CREB1.[9][7] These are described by the authors as mechanistic findings; controlled human trials of finished creams for appearance are limited.

Wikipedia's article states that excessive intake could cause calcium toxicity and notes that its medical claims need more reliable sources.[1] A review of nano-pearl powder in osteogenesis lists mechanistic gaps and safety considerations as open questions.[15]

Few clinical studies on appearance outcomes were found. Most work is laboratory or animal research: pearl extract enhanced fibroblast migration in a wound-healing model,[2] a pearl extract gel was reported to have anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic effects on UVB-irradiated skin cells,[4] and a rat study examined pearl and premature ovarian failure.[16] A registered trial (NCT05571514, recruiting, n=200) is testing mother-of-pearl supplements for postmenopausal osteoporosis, not appearance.[17]
